title: 5 Real-World DFM Case Studies and What Manufacturers Can Learn From Them
summary: Nov 02, 2026 | Explore five real-world DFM case studies showing how manufacturers use AI, design reviews, and supplier collaboration to reduce costs and catch issues earlier.
body_markdown:
Enterprise manufacturers have spent decades compiling standards and lessons learned that guide how to make their products easier and less expensive to manufacture. And yet, applying that knowledge consistently across programs still depends heavily on the availability and judgment of a small group of experienced engineers. Fortunately,[AI tools for mechanical engineers](https://www.colabsoftware.com/ai-tools-for-mechanical-engineers-guide) can now automate some of that routine checking, freeing experienced engineers to focus on complex manufacturing decisions, resolve design issues earlier, and improve designs before they reach production.


**Design for manufacturability (DFM) is an ideal starting point for AI in manufacturing because the requirements, review processes, and measures of success already exist.** AI can help apply company-specific manufacturing knowledge to active designs, while engineers validate the findings and decide what, if anything, needs to be fixed or optimized.


Five examples below illustrate both the early progress of AI-powered DFM checks and the business outcomes that make extending these capabilities across engineering organizations well worth the investment.


## **5 DFM case studies and what manufacturers can learn from them**


Manufacturer Manufacturing-related result Implication for AI and DFM


[Automotive supplier](https://www.colabsoftware.com/post/building-ai-for-dfm) **Over 80% accuracy and relevance** in an initial implementation of AI-powered DFM checks against injection-molding guidelines. **Existing DFM standards provide a testable foundation for AI.** Manufacturers can evaluate automated findings against their own requirements and designs before expanding to other processes.


[INFICON](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/inficon) **First-time-right on one product program** , avoiding an estimated 4–6 weeks of additional development. **Finding an issue only pays off when it prevents another development cycle.** AI checks need to feed into design reviews, where engineers can resolve concerns before drawings, sourcing, and prototypes move forward.


[Mainspring Energy](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/mainspring) **50% lower cost** on an enclosure redesign, with approximately 300 manufacturing drawings reviewed before supplier release. **DFM has significant design-to-cost potential.** An effective AI strategy should help engineers identify manufacturing cost opportunities as well as prevent avoidable defects.


[Schneider Electric](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/schneider-electric) **15% reduction in non-quality costs** for EcoFit Canada, including costs associated with rework and scrap. **Cost of poor quality is a meaningful measure of DFM performance.** AI investments should ultimately be evaluated against downstream manufacturing outcomes, rather than the volume of findings generated.


[Structure Medical](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/structure-medical) **Quoting turnaround reduced from weeks to hours** , with DFM feedback exchanged directly between machining specialists and OEM engineers. **Supplier expertise needs to influence the design before manufacturing commitments are made.** Automating checks has limited value if resolving findings still depends on lengthy supplier exchanges.


## **The first challenge is turning manufacturing knowledge into reliable checks**


Most large manufacturers have no shortage of DFM guidelines. The difficulty is determining which requirements apply to a particular design and checking them consistently across thousands of parts.


[AI-powered engineering search](https://www.colabsoftware.com/operator) can retrieve relevant standards, previous reviews, and supplier recommendations. But that information still needs to be evaluated against the design itself. An injection molding guideline specifying minimum draft, for example, must be translated into a geometric check that accounts for the intended mold pull direction and identifies where the part fails to meet the requirement.


To apply those requirements directly to a model,[AutoReview](https://www.colabsoftware.com/product/autoreview) combines AI-assisted analysis of engineering requirements with deterministic checks on CAD geometry, allowing engineers to examine potential manufacturing problems directly on the model.


CoLab's initial work with an automotive supplier provides an early indication of the approach’s viability. Engineers evaluated the automated findings against their own injection molding guidelines, establishing a basis for improving the checks before expanding to other processes.


Importantly, the quality of an automated DFM check should be judged against the manufacturer’s requirements and actual designs, including the issues it misses and the findings engineers reject. A promising accuracy result is a starting point for validation, but not necessarily a guarantee of manufacturability.


[Read CTO Jeremy Andrews’ account of CoLab’s automotive DFM implementation](https://www.colabsoftware.com/post/building-ai-for-dfm) .


## **More automated feedback won’t necessarily produce better designs**


A manufacturability concern can be technically valid without having an obvious resolution. A supplier may recommend changing a feature to simplify machining, while the design engineer has functional requirements that constrain the available options. Resolving the issue often requires multiple parties to evaluate the trade-off.


That interaction is central to[Structure Medical’s approach to DFM collaboration](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/structure-medical) . Its machining specialists provide feedback directly to OEM engineers during the quoting process, when there is still an opportunity to influence the design and establish how the part will be manufactured.


CoLab supports that collaboration directly on the design. AutoReview findings and human feedback appear as comments and markups attached to the relevant geometry, where engineers and suppliers can discuss proposed changes, assign responsibility, and track issues through resolution. An automated finding becomes part of the same review process as a concern raised by an experienced manufacturing engineer.


AI can identify more issues earlier, but manufacturers also need the collaborative tools and review processes to resolve those findings efficiently. Otherwise, automation risks creating another queue of findings for the same overstretched specialists.


[INFICON's experience](https://www.colabsoftware.com/case-studies/inficon) illustrates a more complete approach. For its NPD team, automated drawing checks were incorporated into a structured review process where engineers assessed findings, assigned responsibility, and verified resolutions. Engineers also examine designs asynchronously before meetings, allowing live discussions to focus on outstanding concerns and the decisions needed to move forward.


As AI increases the number of designs and requirements that can be checked, the capacity to resolve findings becomes increasingly important. Manufacturers need to improve their review processes alongside their automated checks, or risk shifting the bottleneck from identifying problems to deciding what to do about them.


## **The next advantage comes from capturing the decisions behind automated checks**


Automated DFM checks are usually only as useful as the manufacturing requirements they apply. As those requirements evolve, along with supplier capabilities and lessons learned from production, engineering teams need a way to update their checks without manually reprogramming every rule.


Some of the most valuable updates originate in design reviews themselves. An engineer might accept a supplier’s recommendation to change a feature, establishing a more economical manufacturing approach for future designs. Meanwhile, another recommendation might be rejected because it conflicts with a functional requirement. Both decisions contain information that could improve subsequent DFM checks, provided the reasoning is preserved.


Those decisions can be captured directly in CoLab, alongside the design, the original feedback, and the discussion that led to the resolution. The result is a record of the engineering judgment behind a change, including why a recommendation was accepted or rejected.


For large manufacturers, this creates an opportunity to make **design reviews a source of continuously improving manufacturing knowledge** . As CoLab explores in our[argument for starting AI transformation with DFM](https://www.colabsoftware.com/post/ai-in-manufacturing-start-with-dfm) , scaling these capabilities requires far more than simply automating existing checks. Teams also need a way to capture new lessons, validate their broader applicability, and incorporate them into the requirements that guide future designs.


CoLab's[AI Engineering Knowledge Graph](https://www.colabsoftware.com/product/ai-knowledge-graph) helps preserve the connections between designs, review feedback, and engineering decisions. Because this information is captured within CoLab, it can also inform future reviews. AutoReview’s[AI Lessons Learned](https://www.colabsoftware.com/product/ai-lessons-learned) capabilities can surface relevant feedback from previous designs, giving engineers access to both the earlier recommendation and the reasoning behind its resolution.


Of course, a decision made on one part should not automatically become a manufacturing requirement for every subsequent design. Engineers still need to determine whether a lesson is broadly applicable while accounting for exceptions, and then approve changes to company guidelines or automated checks. Ultimately, the ability to capture the original decision provides the information needed to make that assessment on an ongoing, adaptable basis.


## **Making DFM expertise a scalable advantage**


For enterprise manufacturers, an AI DFM check earns its value when engineers can act on the findings and use the resulting decisions to improve future designs.
